subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 11! You already know your way around small multiplication and division facts, and in this unit you will grow those skills into something much more powerful. You will learn to multiply and divide by 10 and 100 in a flash, to break big multiplications apart with the grid method, to handle division that does not come out evenly by using remainders, and to choose the right operation when a problem is dressed up as a real-life story.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 3 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Multiply whole numbers by 10 and 100 and explain the place-value pattern behind it.
Divide whole numbers by 10 and 100 and explain why the digits move to the right.
Use the grid method to multiply a two-digit number by a one-digit number.
Use the grid method to multiply a two-digit number by a two-digit number.
Carry out division that leaves a remainder, and write the answer correctly (for example 47 ÷ 6 = 7 r 5).
Use your multiplication facts to work out division facts quickly.
Interpret a remainder in a real-world story – deciding whether to round up, round down, or share it out.
Read a word problem, choose multiplication or division, solve it, and check that the answer makes sense.

concepts.title: Multiplying by 10 and 100
concepts.explanation:
Multiplying by 10 is one of the most useful shortcuts in all of mathematics, and there is a beautiful pattern behind it. Look at these examples:

Multiplying by 100 follows exactly the same idea, only bigger. Look at these:

When we multiply by 100, every digit moves two places to the left, and we write two zeros to hold the ones and tens places empty. In 5 × 100, the 5 jumps all the way from the ones place to the hundreds place. In 32 × 100, the 3 moves to the thousands place and the 2 moves to the hundreds place, giving 3,200. Once you understand that the digits are sliding along the place-value columns, you will never be confused about how many zeros to write. Multiplying by 10 shifts one place; multiplying by 100 shifts two places.
concepts.example: Here is a real example from daily life. If one pencil costs 30 cents, then 10 pencils cost 30 × 10 = 300 cents, which is 3 dollars. If one box of crayons costs 2 dollars, then 100 boxes cost 2 × 100 = 200 dollars. When Khadija buys tea in bulk for Nuur Academy, she uses exactly this trick to work out the cost of ten packets or a hundred packets in her head.

concepts.title: Dividing by 10 and 100
concepts.explanation:
Division by 10 is the opposite, or inverse, of multiplication by 10. If multiplying by 10 slides every digit one place to the left, then dividing by 10 slides every digit one place to the right. Look at these examples:

Dividing by 100 moves every digit two places to the right, and removes two zeros from a number that ends in two zeros. Look at these:
concepts.example: This is extremely handy with money. If 10 notebooks cost 45 dollars, then one notebook costs 45 ÷ 10 = 4 dollars 50 cents. If 100 stickers cost 350 dollars, then one sticker costs 350 ÷ 100 = 3 dollars 50 cents. Because multiplying and dividing by 10 and 100 are inverse operations, you can always check one with the other. If 24 × 10 = 240, then 240 ÷ 10 must equal 24. Whenever you are unsure, undo your work with the opposite operation and see if you land back where you started.

concepts.title: The Grid Method for Multiplication
concepts.explanation:
When numbers get bigger, multiplying them in your head becomes hard. The grid method (sometimes called the box method) makes it easy again by breaking a big multiplication into small, friendly pieces. The idea rests on place value: you split each number into its tens and ones, multiply the parts separately, then add the pieces back together.

Let us multiply 34 × 6 step by step. First, split 34 into 30 and 4. Draw a grid with one row and two columns, and write 30 and 4 along the top, with 6 down the side:

Now add the two partial products: 180 + 24 = 204. So 34 × 6 = 204. Notice how we turned one hard multiplication into two easy ones. Multiplying 30 × 6 is really just 3 × 6 = 18 with a zero added, and 4 × 6 = 24 is a fact you already know.

The grid method works for even larger numbers, such as a two-digit number times a two-digit number. Let us try 26 × 38. Split 26 into 20 and 6, and split 38 into 30 and 8. Now the grid has two rows and two columns, giving four partial products:

Add them all together: 600 + 180 + 160 + 48 = 988. So 26 × 38 = 988. It may look like a lot of steps, but every single one is an easy multiplication and a simple addition. The grid keeps everything tidy so you never lose track of a piece. This is far safer than trying to do it all in your head at once.
concepts.example: The grid method is not just for exercises. Suppose 28 students at Nuur Academy each need 15 coloured pencils. To find the total, work out 28 × 15. Split 28 into 20 and 8, and 15 into 10 and 5: (20 × 10) + (8 × 10) + (20 × 5) + (8 × 5) = 200 + 80 + 100 + 40 = 420 coloured pencils. The grid turned a real classroom question into four easy sums.

concepts.title: Division with Remainders
concepts.explanation:
When you divide, the numbers do not always fit together evenly. The amount left over is called the remainder. Understanding remainders is one of the most important ideas in this unit, because in real life things very often do not share out perfectly.

Let us look at 17 ÷ 5. How many whole groups of 5 fit inside 17? We can fit 3 groups, because 5 × 3 = 15. That uses up 15, and 17 − 15 = 2 are left over. So we write 17 ÷ 5 = 3 remainder 2, which is often shortened to 3 r 2. The 3 is the quotient (the number of whole groups) and the 2 is the remainder (what could not be shared).

Here is a careful step-by-step method using 47 ÷ 6:

Find how many groups of 6 fit into 47. Think through the six times table: 6 × 7 = 42 (less than 47) and 6 × 8 = 48 (too big). So 7 groups of 6 fit.

Find how much is left over. 47 − 42 = 5.

Write the answer with the remainder. 47 ÷ 6 = 7 r 5.
concepts.example: Notice how your multiplication facts did all the hard work. Knowing the times tables well makes division with remainders quick, because you are really just asking, what is the largest multiple of the divisor that still fits? For example, to solve 52 ÷ 8, recall that 8 × 6 = 48 (fits) and 8 × 7 = 56 (too big). So 52 ÷ 8 = 6 with 52 − 48 = 4 left over, giving 6 r 4. An important safety check: the remainder must always be smaller than the divisor. If your remainder is equal to or bigger than the number you divided by, you could have fit another whole group in, so go back and try again.

concepts.title: Interpreting Remainders in Real Life
concepts.explanation:
A remainder is not just a number at the end of a sum – in a real problem it means something, and what you do with it depends on the story. This is where many learners slip, so read this concept carefully.

Imagine 29 students need to be put into teams of 5. We work out 29 ÷ 5 = 5 r 4. We can make 5 complete teams (that uses 25 students) and 4 students are left over. What should happen to those 4? Depending on the situation you might: add them to existing teams to make some teams a little larger, form one smaller team of 4, or ask them to be helpers and referees. The maths gives you 5 r 4, but you decide what the remainder means.

Sometimes the remainder tells you to round up. If 156 students are going on a trip to Mombasa and each bus carries 52 students, then 156 ÷ 52 = 3 exactly, so 3 buses are enough. But if there were 160 students, 160 ÷ 52 = 3 r 4. Those 4 extra students still need a seat, so you cannot leave them behind – you need a 4th bus. When every item or person must be carried, you round the number of groups up.
concepts.example: At other times the remainder is simply thrown away, or rounded down. If Farah has 50 shillings and each party bag costs 4 shillings, then 50 ÷ 4 = 12 r 2. She can buy only 12 bags, because the leftover 2 shillings is not enough for a thirteenth bag. Here the remainder is money she keeps, and the answer to how many bags is 12. So always ask yourself: does this story want me to round up, round down, or share the leftover out? The correct choice comes from the real-world meaning, not from the numbers alone.

concepts.title: Multiplication and Division Are Inverses
concepts.explanation:
Multiplication and division are like two sides of the same coin – each one undoes the other. This idea is called being inverse operations, and it is one of the most useful tools you have. Every multiplication fact hides a pair of division facts inside it. These four related facts are called a fact family.

Take the fact 6 × 7 = 42. From this single fact we instantly know four things:

7 × 6 = 42 (the order of the factors does not change the product – this is the commutative property)

You have now met six big ideas: multiplying by 10 and 100, dividing by 10 and 100, the grid method for larger multiplications, division with remainders, interpreting those remainders in real stories, and the way multiplication and division work as inverses. These ideas are not separate islands – they support one another. When Hassan works out how many crates of 12 mangoes he can fill from a pick of 245, he divides, interprets the remainder to know how many mangoes are left loose, and can check his crate count by multiplying back. When Zahra prices 100 packets of dates for the shop, she multiplies by 100 in a single move.
concepts.example: The very best way to lock these ideas into your memory is to use them out loud with real things around your home. Count how many legs there are on a group of goats by multiplying. Share a bowl of dates among your family and notice the remainder. Work out the cost of ten of something at the market. Every time you do this, your number sense grows stronger, and the harder maths in later units will feel much easier. Now let us practise together with some worked examples.

methods.title: The grid method (two-digit by one-digit)
steps: Split the two-digit number into tens and ones (34 becomes 30 and 4).
Multiply each part by the one-digit number (30 × 6 = 180 and 4 × 6 = 24).
Add the partial products (180 + 24 = 204).

methods.title: The grid method (two-digit by two-digit)
steps: Split both numbers into tens and ones (26 → 20 and 6; 38 → 30 and 8).
Fill all four boxes: 20 × 30, 6 × 30, 20 × 8, 6 × 8.
Add the four partial products together (600 + 180 + 160 + 48 = 988).

methods.title: Division with a remainder
methods.example: Use the grid method to calculate 27 × 5.
steps: Find the largest multiple of the divisor that fits inside the dividend.
Subtract it to find what is left over — that is the remainder.
Write the answer as a whole number with the remainder (47 ÷ 6 = 7 r 5).
Check: the remainder must be smaller than the divisor.

methods.title: Grid method, two-digit by two-digit
methods.example: Use the grid method to calculate 32 × 24.
steps: Split 32 into 30 and 2, and 24 into 20 and 4.
The four partial products are: 30 × 20 = 600, 2 × 20 = 40, 30 × 4 = 120, and 2 × 4 = 8.

methods.title: Division with a remainder
steps: Look for the largest multiple of 9 that fits inside 64.
Since 9 × 7 = 63 (fits) and 9 × 8 = 72 (too big), 7 groups fit.
The remainder is 64 − 63 = 1.

methods.title: A remainder you must round up
methods.example: A baker has 53 cookies and packs them into boxes of 8. How many full boxes can she make, and how many cookies are left over?
steps: Since 8 × 6 = 48 (fits) and 8 × 7 = 56 (too big), 6 boxes are full and 53 − 48 = 5 cookies are left over.
So she makes 6 full boxes with 5 cookies left over.
(If the question had asked how many boxes she needs to hold every cookie, she would need a 7th box for those 5.)

workedExamples.title: Multiplying by 10 and 100
workedExamples.solution: For 18 × 10, slide every digit one place left and add a zero: 18 × 10 = 180. For 25 × 100, slide every digit two places left and add two zeros: 25 × 100 = 2,500.

workedExamples.title: Dividing by 10 and 100
workedExamples.solution: For 420 ÷ 10, slide every digit one place right, removing one zero: 420 ÷ 10 = 42. For 600 ÷ 100, slide every digit two places right, removing two zeros: 600 ÷ 100 = 6.

workedExamples.title: Grid method, two-digit by one-digit
workedExamples.prompt: Use the grid method to calculate 27 × 5.
workedExamples.solution: Split 27 into 20 and 7. Then 20 × 5 = 100 and 7 × 5 = 35. Add the partial products: 100 + 35 = 135. So 27 × 5 = 135.

workedExamples.title: Grid method, two-digit by two-digit
workedExamples.prompt: Use the grid method to calculate 32 × 24.
workedExamples.solution: Split 32 into 30 and 2, and 24 into 20 and 4. The four partial products are: 30 × 20 = 600, 2 × 20 = 40, 30 × 4 = 120, and 2 × 4 = 8. Add them: 600 + 40 + 120 + 8 = 768. So 32 × 24 = 768.

workedExamples.title: Division with a remainder
workedExamples.solution: Look for the largest multiple of 9 that fits inside 64. Since 9 × 7 = 63 (fits) and 9 × 8 = 72 (too big), 7 groups fit. The remainder is 64 − 63 = 1. So 64 ÷ 9 = 7 r 1. Check: the remainder 1 is smaller than the divisor 9, so this is correct.

workedExamples.title: A remainder you must round up
workedExamples.prompt: A baker has 53 cookies and packs them into boxes of 8. How many full boxes can she make, and how many cookies are left over?
workedExamples.solution: 53 ÷ 8. Since 8 × 6 = 48 (fits) and 8 × 7 = 56 (too big), 6 boxes are full and 53 − 48 = 5 cookies are left over. So she makes 6 full boxes with 5 cookies left over. (If the question had asked how many boxes she needs to hold every cookie, she would need a 7th box for those 5.)

workedExamples.title: Using a fact family to divide
workedExamples.prompt: A teacher has 42 pencils to share equally among 6 students. How many pencils does each student get?
workedExamples.solution: This is 42 ÷ 6. Ask, what number times 6 makes 42? Since 6 × 7 = 42, the answer is 42 ÷ 6 = 7 pencils each. There is no remainder, because 42 is an exact multiple of 6.

workedExamples.title: Choosing the operation in a word problem
workedExamples.prompt: A baker uses 3 eggs to make one batch of cookies. How many eggs are needed for 8 batches?
workedExamples.solution: The word each and the idea of repeating equal groups tell us to multiply: 8 batches × 3 eggs = 8 × 3 = 24 eggs. Check that it makes sense: more batches need more eggs, and 24 is bigger than 3, so the answer is sensible.

activities.title: The Zero Slide (Multiply and Divide by 10 and 100)
activities.materials: number cards 0 to 9 and a place-value chart with columns for hundreds, tens and ones (draw one on paper).
steps: Place a two-digit number on the chart, for example 45.
Show × 10 by sliding every digit one column to the left and writing a zero in the ones column.
Show × 100 by sliding every digit two columns to the left and writing two zeros.
Now reverse it: slide the digits back to the right to show ÷ 10 and ÷ 100. Say what you notice about the zeros.
Watching the digits slide helps you see that multiplying and dividing by 10 and 100 is all about place value, not just adding zeros.

activities.title: Build a Grid (Box Method with Household Objects)
activities.materials: grid paper or a hand-drawn box, a pencil.
steps: Choose a two-digit by one-digit multiplication, such as 34 × 6.
Draw a grid and split 34 into 30 and 4 along the top, with 6 down the side.
Fill each box: 30 × 6 = 180 and 4 × 6 = 24.
Add the partial products to find the answer, then check it a second way (for example by repeated addition of 34).
Try harder ones next, like 26 × 38, and see how the grid keeps all four partial products tidy.

activities.title: Division Detective (Remainders with Counters)
activities.materials: a handful of small objects – dry beans, stones, or bottle caps.
steps: Count out 23 objects.
Arrange them into equal groups of 4. How many complete groups can you make?
Count how many objects are left over.
Write the division sentence: 23 ÷ 4 = 5 r 3. Then try new numbers of objects and new group sizes.
Seeing the leftover objects with your own eyes makes the meaning of a remainder crystal clear.

activities.title: Market Multiplication (Family Task)
activities.materials: a real or pretend market, with stones standing in for shillings and household items for goods.
steps: Set a price for one item, for example 12 shillings for a bag of dates.
A family member asks: How much for 10 bags? For 100 bags? Use your place-value slide to answer.
Now share out goods: 47 dates into bags of 6. How many full bags, and how many dates are left?
Talk about what to do with the leftover dates in real life.

activities.title: Fact Family Fold (Multiplication and Division Game)
steps: Pick three numbers that make a fact, such as 6, 7 and 42.
Write all four members of the fact family: 6 × 7 = 42, 7 × 6 = 42, 42 ÷ 6 = 7, 42 ÷ 7 = 6.
Fold the paper to hide the answer to one fact and challenge a partner to say it.
Make ten different fact-family cards and quiz each other to build speed.
This game shows you that every multiplication fact you know gives you a division fact for free.

activities.title: Remainder Investigation
activities.materials: paper, a pencil, and a die or number cards.
steps: Roll or pick a two-digit number to be the dividend.
Divide it by 5 and record the remainder. Repeat for many different numbers.
List all the remainders you get. Which remainders are possible when you divide by 5? (You should never see 5 or more.)
Now try dividing by 4 and by 6, and describe the pattern in the possible remainders.

After your activities, talk or write about: Which activity helped you understand the grid method or remainders best? What was the trickiest part? What would you like more practice with? Share your answers with your teacher at your next session.

rules.title: Key rule 1
rules.text: Multiplying by 10 and 100 × 10: every digit moves one place to the left; add one zero. 24 × 10 = 240. × 100: every digit moves two places to the left; add two zeros. 24 × 100 = 2,400.

rules.title: Key rule 2
rules.text: Dividing by 10 and 100 ÷ 10: every digit moves one place to the right; remove one zero. 240 ÷ 10 = 24. ÷ 100: every digit moves two places to the right; remove two zeros. 2,400 ÷ 100 = 24.

rules.title: Remainder Rule
rules.text: The remainder is what is left over after making as many equal groups as possible. The remainder is always smaller than the divisor.

realProblems.prompt: A bus can carry 52 students. If 160 students go on a trip to Nairobi, how many buses are needed? Explain what you do with the remainder.
realProblems.answer: 160 ÷ 52 = 3 remainder 4. Three buses fill exactly 156 students, but the remaining 4 students still need a seat, so a 4th bus is needed — 4 buses in total.

reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 89 ÷ 10 = 8 remainder 9. There are 8 full bags, with 9 apples left over.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain, with an example, why the remainder in a division can never be as large as the divisor.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: If the remainder were equal to or larger than the divisor, you could make one more full group. For example, in 23 ÷ 4, if the remainder were 4 or more, that would mean another group of 4 fits — so the remainder must always be smaller than the divisor. 23 ÷ 4 = 5 r 3, and 3 is less than 4.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A shopkeeper buys 100 boxes of dates for 450 shillings each. Then she wants the cost of just one box if instead 100 boxes together cost 4,500 shillings. Work out 4,500 ÷ 100.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 4,500 ÷ 100 = 45. Dividing by 100 moves every digit two places to the right, so one box costs 45 shillings.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Multiplication and Division Are Inverses.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Multiplication and division are like two sides of the same coin – each one undoes the other. This idea is called being inverse operations, and it is one of the most useful tools you have. Every multiplication fact hides a pair of division facts inside it. questions.question: Use the grid method to calculate 27 × 5.
questions.hint: Work it out step by step, using the Unit 11 methods.
questions.explanation: Split 27 into 20 and 7. Then 20 × 5 = 100 and 7 × 5 = 35. Add the partial products: 100 + 35 = 135. So 27 × 5 = 135.

questions.question: Use the grid method to calculate 32 × 24.
questions.hint: Work it out step by step, using the Unit 11 methods.
questions.explanation: Split 32 into 30 and 2, and 24 into 20 and 4. The four partial products are: 30 × 20 = 600, 2 × 20 = 40, 30 × 4 = 120, and 2 × 4 = 8. Add them: 600 + 40 + 120 + 8 = 768. So 32 × 24 = 768.

selfAssessment: I can multiply whole numbers by 10 and 100 and explain the place-value pattern behind it.
I can divide whole numbers by 10 and 100 and explain why the digits move to the right.
I can use the grid method to multiply a two-digit number by a one-digit number.
I can use the grid method to multiply a two-digit number by a two-digit number.
I can carry out division that leaves a remainder, and write the answer correctly (for example 47 ÷ 6 = 7 r 5).
I can use your multiplication facts to work out division facts quickly.
I can interpret a remainder in a real-world story – deciding whether to round up, round down, or share it out.
I can read a word problem, choose multiplication or division, solve it, and check that the answer makes sense.
